title: Crisis team prepares for worst: Police unit offers support after a tragedy
article: In any tragedy, the person who has lost his life inevitably becomes "the victim." But there may be countless other victims -- the family and friends who have lost someone dear.
"Initially, it's disbelief," said Staff Sgt. George Rocks of the Calgary Police Service homicide unit, about the reaction of relatives to a death.
"It's not like television, where there are people standing around screaming and yelling. It's very quiet, very passive disbelief. It takes a while to set in."
When the shock wears off and the reality of the tragedy hits home, though, Rocks said there's a group of crisis workers ready to comfort survivors.
"Usually, people don't want anything. It's not real," said Rocks. "We offer (the counselling service) anyway."
He said the police crisis team is also available later on. "We know what they're going through. They have to say: \`Yeah, I want to talk to somebody.' "

When Samer Jaber was killed in November -- stabbed three times in a stairwell at Lester B. Pearson High School in the northeast -- crisis workers were sent to the hospital where Jaber's family had gathered.
"They provide an invaluable service to the investigators and the families," Rocks said.
Police also moved crisis workers into gear in the case of Arthur George Provencal, 34, the man shot and killed Dec. 23 by police during an attempted robbery and hostage taking at a downtown pharmacy.

Calgary police called their Ottawa counterparts to have crisis workers with the Ontario family when officers called to break the news of Provencal's death. "We never leave people dangling," Rocks said.
Jane Eddison heads up the team of five Calgary Police Service clinical social workers who go to the aid of people suddenly finding themselves in tragic situations.
Team members carry police radios and are ready to help at all times.
"Our rule is to immediately work with these people who are left trying to grapple with this incredible news they've been delivered," said Eddison.
"It's that immediacy that's so valuable. We see what's traumatized them.

"We try to get people back to a former level of coping and managing. It leaves you with a sense of vulnerability and fear. It's not like you can inoculate for these tragedies. You realize the fragility of life."
Eddison said people dealing with tragedy may lose their concentration for everyday life or lose their memories. They might believe they are going crazy.
"The reactions can be from silence. . . to wailing and screaming," she said. "All of it is trying to come to terms with dreadful news."
Eddison said if a relative of a homicide victim is under the care of a psychologist, that professional may be brought in to extend the crisis unit's help for the individual.
Other people may be referred to social workers or bereavement groups.
"Talking to a professional helps put the tragedy into a manageable place in their lives," said Eddison.
"We assess the situation and make a determination. For people with really strong religious connections, we refer to the clergy."
That aid is also extended to people who may have witnessed a crime, such as a homicide, she said. "We will work with people no matter what stage of the process they're at."
Rocks said the medical examiner's office also has staff nurses trained to help grieving families when autopsies on sudden death victims are performed.
